subject: Chemistry
title: Flame Tests: Colors from Metal Ions
description: One-minute skill: Flame Tests: Colors from Metal Ions.

hook.text: Hold different metal salts over a flame: sodium burns orange, copper burns green, lithium burns red.

buildup.text: Heat excites electrons in metal atoms, bumping them to higher energy levels.

discovery.text: When electrons fall back down, they emit photons of specific wavelengths—visible as distinct colors.

twist.text: Every element has a unique spectrum. That's how astronomers identify what distant stars are made of.

climax.text: Fireworks use this same principle. Strontium for red, barium for green, copper for blue.

punchline.text: Heat metal, electrons jump, light appears. Each element has its own color.

quiz.question: Why do different metals produce different flame colors?
options: Each element's electrons emit photons at unique wavelengths
Different metals burn at different temperatures
The flames reflect the metal's natural color

details.summary: Flame tests identify metal ions by the characteristic colors they emit when electrons absorb thermal energy and release it as visible light. Each element produces a unique spectral signature: sodium glows yellow, copper green, lithium red, and potassium violet.
details.whyItMatters: Flame tests provide rapid qualitative identification of metals in chemistry labs and forensic investigations. The underlying principle also powers fireworks and astronomical spectroscopy.
takeaways: Each metal ion emits a characteristic color when heated in a flame
The colors result from specific electron energy level transitions
Flame tests are the chemical basis for firework color design

faq.question: Why does each metal produce a unique flame color?
faq.answer: Each element has a unique arrangement of electron energy levels. When heated, electrons jump to higher levels and fall back, emitting photons at specific wavelengths. The wavelength determines the color. Since energy levels are element-specific, colors are unique identifiers.

faq.question: Why is sodium's yellow flame so dominant that it masks other elements?
faq.answer: Sodium emits an extremely intense yellow doublet at 589 nanometers. Even trace sodium contamination, common from handling, overwhelms subtler flame colors. Chemists use cobalt blue glass to filter out sodium's yellow and reveal other elements beneath.
